references.text: Isaiah sees the Lord's glory and hears the seraphim cry: 'Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory', which directly connects to Jesus' prayer that God's name be glorified and the heavenly voice confirming that the name has been glorified.

The Lord says: 'For my own sake, for my own sake I do this, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I give not to another', which mirrors Jesus' prayer to glorify the name and God's response that He Himself will glorify it.

The psalm cries out: 'Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your steadfast love and for your faithfulness', which is a direct parallel to Jesus' prayer that God's name be glorified above human honor.

In His high-priestly prayer, Jesus prays: 'Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that the Son may glorify you', and later 'I have glorified you on earth... Now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed', which is the direct theological extension of the prayer's theme in John 12:28.

Shortly after Judas has gone out, Jesus says: 'Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once', which shows the immediate connection between Jesus' death, God's glorification, and the coming glorification.
